O.outcome_detail: Observed Cognitive Shift on the Bloom ordinal scale

cells.quote: When instructed to make a task “Harder,” both models demonstrate a strong upward cognitive shift (an average OCS of 1.582 for the coder model and 1.762 for the general model). However, an asymmetry appears when attempting to reduce cognitive demand. Under the general “Easier” prompt, both models still produce positive OCS scores (0.715 and 0.194), showing that a request for lower surface difficulty does not necessarily yield lower Bloom-level demand.
cells.note: The study evaluates generated programming-task mutations rather than learners; learner expertise, age, setting, and duration are not stated.

O.outcome_detail: Observed Cognitive Shift and Target Zone Accuracy

result.effect: OCS—Coder: 1.495 vs 0.103; General: 2.146 vs -0.134. TZA—Coder: 0.634 vs 0.251; General: 0.792 vs 0.292

cells.quote: When instructed to make a task “Harder,” both models demonstrate a strong upward cognitive shift (an average OCS of 1.582 for the coder model and 1.762 for the general model). These shifts mirror the behavior observed when models are explicitly prompted to target a “Higher” Bloom’s level. Comparing this to the targeted “Lower” Bloom’s setting reveals that Bloom context slightly mitigates this issue (the general model achieved a marginal negative shift -0.134), but the overarching resistance remains. As shown in Table 2, both models perform well when targeting “Higher” levels. The general model succeeds 79.2% of the time, outperforming the coder model’s 63.4% success rate. By contrast, targeting “Lower” levels exposes a clear weakness, with overall accuracy dropping below 30% for both models.
cells.note: The study reports model-generated task control, not learner learning outcomes.

O.outcome_detail: Fisher’s Discriminant Ratio for Harder/Easier instruction separability

result.effect: General peak FDR ≈ 0.0303 at Layer 29; coder peak FDR ≈ 0.0108 at Layer 28

cells.quote: For general difficulty instructions, its peak FDR remains low (≈ 0.0108 at Layer 28), indicating more overlapping activation distributions under this linear diagnostic. ... The general model displays a more separated distribution between “Harder” and “Easier” along the projected axis. The coder model shows more overlap and higher variance, which is consistent with its lower FDR score.
cells.note: The comparison is a representation diagnostic between two matched Qwen3-Next models; no learner population or instructional setting is stated.

O.outcome_detail: Fisher’s Discriminant Ratio for Higher/Lower Bloom-target instruction separability

result.effect: General peak FDR ≈ 0.0224 at Layer 28; coder peak FDR at Layer 36, with substantial overlap

cells.quote: For the general model, the peak separability depth for difficulty instructions (“Harder”/“Easier”) and Bloom-target instructions (“Higher”/“Lower”) is nearly identical. Specifically, the model reaches peak linear separability at Layer 29 (FDR ≈ 0.0303) for difficulty and Layer 28 (FDR≈ 0.0224) for Bloom targets. ... Meanwhile, the coder model, which delays this peak separability until Layer 36, still shows substantial overlap between the “Higher” and “Lower” targets.
cells.note: The study describes layer-wise residual-stream probing, not an instructional intervention with learners.

O.outcome_detail: projected activation distribution for “Higher” versus “Lower” Bloom targets

result.effect: Qualitative: substantial coder overlap; no numeric projection effect reported

cells.quote: This pattern of stronger diagnostic separation in the general model continues in the context of Bloom targets. As illustrated in Figure 3, the general model maintains a sharper projected distribution at its middle-layer peak. Meanwhile, the coder model, which delays this peak separability until Layer 36, still shows substantial overlap between the “Higher” and “Lower” targets.
